chunks.section: Zeroth-Order Riemannian Optimization on Fixed-Rank Manifolds for LLM Fine-Tuning
chunks.text: Xinjue Wang Affiliation: Department of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University Xiuheng Wang † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: School of Future Technology, South China University of Technology Yejun Zhang Affiliation: Department of Computer Science, Aalto University Sergiy A. Vorobyov Affiliation: Department of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University Esa Ollila Affiliation: Department of Information and Communications Engineering, Aalto University

Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Achiam et al., 2023 ) . Fine-tuning these models on downstream tasks is crucial for their practical deployment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) have emerged as a practical solution, training low-rank updates while keeping pretrained weights frozen ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024a ) . However, first-order optimization still incurs substantial memory overhead from storing activations for backpropagation, especially in long-context settings where activations dominate memory. To enhance memory efficiency, zeroth-order (ZO) fine-tuning methods ( Malladi et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) estimate descent directions from function values without backpropagated gradients, avoiding the activation storage required by backward passes ( Spall, 1992 ) .

Recent low-rank ZO fine-tuning methods combine these two directions by restricting the finite-difference search through low-rank perturbations, adapter factors, gradient estimators, or random subspaces ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Song and Li, 2026 ) . Factor-based approaches constrain the learned update through adapter coordinates, whereas low-rank perturbation methods constrain individual ZO steps. These two branches of methods differ in the way of constructing low-rank additive update matrices when optimizing a fixed-rank update matrix. Factor-based adaptation uses a factorized update Δ ​ 𝑾 = 𝑩 ​ 𝑨 \Delta\boldsymbol{W}=\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{A} and optimizes over ( 𝑩 , 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{A}) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . This representation is nonunique, since ( 𝑩 ​ 𝑸 ) ​ ( 𝑸 − 1 ​ 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B}\boldsymbol{Q})(\boldsymbol{Q}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}) gives the same update for any invertible 𝑸 \boldsymbol{Q} . Low-rank perturbation and random-subspace methods instead use restricted finite-difference directions or estimators to construct each ZO step ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) . For example, low-rank perturbation methods form each step from a sampled rank- r r direction 𝑼 ​ 𝑽 ⊤ \boldsymbol{U}\boldsymbol{V}^{\top} , while random-subspace variants restrict the step direction to a prescribed low-dimensional subspace ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . As a result, factor-based methods optimize a non-unique parameterization, while perturbation and subspace methods restrict each ZO search direction.

To tackle these issues, we propose to optimize Δ ​ 𝑾 \Delta\boldsymbol{W} as a fixed-rank matrix variable formulated on a Riemannian manifold. Consider one selected weight matrix with frozen pretrained value 𝑾 0 \boldsymbol{W}_{0} . At iteration t t , the adapted weight is written as 𝑾 t = 𝑾 0 + Δ ​ 𝑾 t \boldsymbol{W}_{t}=\boldsymbol{W}_{0}+\Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{t} , with Δ 𝑾 t ∈ ℳ r m × n , t = 0 , … , T , \displaystyle\Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{t}\in\mathcal{M}_{r}^{m\times n},\qquad t=0,\ldots,T, (1) where ℳ r m × n \mathcal{M}_{r}^{m\times n} denotes the manifold of rank- r r matrices in ℝ m × n \mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , with r ≪ min ⁡ { m , n } r\ll\min\{m,n\} . Thus, for this block, the update trajectory stays on the same fixed-rank manifold. This turns fixed-rank structure from a property of an individual ZO step into a constraint on the persistent update trajectory. Building on this fixed-rank update trajectory, we propose a forward-only Riemannian ZO fine-tuning framework. At each step, we project a random matrix onto the current tangent space, normalize it, and retract the update back to the rank- r r manifold to build the ZO Riemannian gradient. We use this gradient to design Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and a smoothed variant (ZO-RGD-S). Figure 1 illustrates the tangent random matrix and the retracted update for one representative matrix block. We summarize the contributions as follows: 1. We formulate forward-only LLM fine-tuning as optimization of persistent additive updates on fixed-rank matrix manifolds. For each selected matrix block, the update trajectory is maintained on a prescribed rank- r r manifold, so the rank constraint is imposed on the optimization state rather than only on an individual ZO step.

2. We show that tangent projection makes the finite-difference perturbation scale depend on the rank and layer shape, and correct this mismatch with a normalized tangent estimator that needs only two forward passes and no additional retractions per step. Building on this estimator, we develop ZO-RGD and its smoothed variant ZO-RGD-S, which recursively smooths the finite-difference scalar at the same forward cost. 3. We prove that the implemented ambient finite difference agrees with its retracted counterpart to leading order, and that the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation up to an 𝒪 ⁡ ( ϵ 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2}) bias. Building on these properties, we establish a nonasymptotic convergence guarantee for ZO-RGD, conditional on regularity of the realized trajectory. 4. We evaluate the proposed methods across model families and downstream tasks against existing forward-only baselines. The results show competitive performance, with gains in several settings.

LoRA adapts a frozen pretrained model by adding a low-rank update to selected weight matrices ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . This idea has led to a large family of PEFT methods, including weight-decomposed adaptation ( Liu et al., 2024a ) , adaptive rank allocation and learning-rate asymmetry ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ) , nonzero initialization and analyses of low-rank training dynamics ( Li et al., 2025 ; Yaras et al., 2024 ) , tensorized update parameterizations ( Yang et al., 2024c ) , rank-one or high-rank structured variants ( Sheng et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) , low-rank gradient projection ( Zhao et al., 2024a ) , and broader PEFT surveys ( Yang et al., 2024a ) . These methods establish low-rank updates as an effective adaptation object. In a forward-only ZO setting, we ask a different question: whether the update matrix itself can be the constrained optimization state, rather than representing it through nonunique factor coordinates.

Classical ZO theory studies simultaneous perturbation, Gaussian or spherical smoothing, and two-point randomized estimators ( Spall, 1992 ; Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ; Duchi et al., 2015 ; Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017 ; Shamir, 2017 ; Berahas et al., 2022 ; Balasubramanian and Ghadimi, 2022 ) . MeZO showed that such forward-only estimates can fine-tune LLMs while avoiding activation-gradient storage ( Malladi et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent work has expanded the optimizer and benchmark landscape through large-scale studies ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , benchmark-oriented analyses ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , random-subspace or low-rank perturbation methods ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ) , and variants that use curvature or projected-alignment information ( Zhao et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Mi et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches explore sparse perturbations ( Liu et al., 2024b ) and step-size adaptation based on batch-loss variability ( Dang et al., 2025 ) . LOZO ( Chen et al., 2025 ) is the closest predecessor because it introduces low-rank structure into ZO estimation for LLMs. The distinction is where the structure lives: LOZO forms a low-rank estimator or subspace update, whereas the proposed algorithms construct their random matrices in the tangent space of the current fixed-rank updates.

chunks.section: Riemannian optimization on fixed-rank matrix manifolds.
chunks.text: Fixed-rank matrix manifolds, tangent projections, and retractions are standard tools for optimizing low-rank matrices without exposing redundant factor gauges ( Absil et al., 2008 ; Vandereycken, 2013 ; Wei et al., 2016 ) . Riemannian ZO optimization studies stochastic optimization over Riemannian submanifolds embedded in Euclidean space when only noisy function evaluations are available ( Li et al., 2022 ) . Recent deep-learning work uses this geometry to optimize low-rank weights directly or to design Riemannian low-rank optimizers and preconditioners ( Bian et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Pilanci, 2024 ; Bogachev et al., 2025 ; Mo et al., 2025 ) . RoZO ( Song and Li, 2026 ) is a closely related concurrent work that combines ZO optimization with geometry induced by low-rank adapter factors, while our method takes the matrix update itself as the optimization variable on the fixed-rank manifold. Riemannian ZO methods establish convergence for exponential-map or retraction-based finite differences under geometric and smoothness assumptions ( Li et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2024 ) . Structure-preserving metrics have also been proposed to address geodesic incompleteness ( Ma and Huang, 2026 ) .

For a stochastic objective f ⁡ ( 𝑿 ) = 𝔼 ξ ​ [ F ⁡ ( 𝑿 , ξ ) ] f(\boldsymbol{X})=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[F(\boldsymbol{X};\xi)] , ZO methods estimate descent directions from function values. Given a data realization ξ \xi and a random matrix 𝒁 \boldsymbol{Z} with i.i.d. standard Gaussian entries, the two-point estimator is ∇ ^ ​ F ​ ( 𝑿 , ξ ) = F ⁡ ( 𝑿 + ϵ ​ 𝒁 , ξ ) − F ⁡ ( 𝑿 − ϵ ​ 𝒁 , ξ ) 2 ​ ϵ ​ 𝒁 , \displaystyle\widehat{\nabla}F(\boldsymbol{X};\xi)=\frac{F(\boldsymbol{X}+\epsilon\boldsymbol{Z};\xi)-F(\boldsymbol{X}-\epsilon\boldsymbol{Z};\xi)}{2\epsilon}\,\boldsymbol{Z}, (2) where ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 controls the perturbation radius ( Duchi et al., 2015 ; Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017 ; Shamir, 2017 ; Berahas et al., 2022 ; Balasubramanian and Ghadimi, 2022 ) . The scalar difference estimates a directional derivative, together with 𝒁 \boldsymbol{Z} , gives a randomized gradient estimate. MeZO uses two forward passes and regenerates 𝒁 \boldsymbol{Z} from seeds to avoid backpropagation and storing perturbations ( Malladi et al., 2023 ) .

This section evaluates ZO-RGD and ZO-RGD-S as forward-only fine-tuning methods. Section 6.2 compares them against cited MeZO and LOZO results on the eleven-task OPT suite at 13B and 30B, the scale at which those baselines report their main results. Section 6.3 removes the reporting asymmetries of cited numbers with a self-run comparison in which every method shares the same protocol, checkpoint rule, and seeds. Section 6.4 tests whether the gains carry over to Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Section 6.5 isolates the geometric ingredients of the method through controlled ablations and reports the computational price of projection and retraction. Full configurations, per-seed values, the complete OPT-1.3B comparison, and further diagnostics are in Appendix D .

We formulate forward-only LLM fine-tuning as optimization of persistent additive updates on fixed-rank matrix manifolds, so that the rank constraint is imposed on the optimization state rather than on individual ZO steps. ZO-RGD estimates the Riemannian gradient from two forward passes with normalized tangent finite differences and retracts each update onto the manifold. ZO-RGD-S adds recursive smoothing of the finite-difference scalar at the same cost. We show that the ambient finite difference agrees with its retracted counterpart to leading order, that the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation up to an 𝒪 ⁡ ( ϵ 2 ) \mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2}) bias, and that ZO-RGD admits a nonasymptotic convergence guarantee conditional on trajectory regularity. Both variants are competitive with strong forward-only baselines on the OPT suite, under a controlled symmetric protocol, and on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, with gains in several settings that mechanism tests attribute to tangent normalization and the manifold parameterization.

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist in implementing the methods, proving the conditional convergence result, and to improve the readability of the paper. We have not used generative AI tools for any other task with required disclosure. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: the code was tested by the authors, and all text edits were checked to preserve the technical content. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

This paper proposes a memory-efficient, forward-only optimizer for fine-tuning large language models and evaluates it on publicly available pretrained models (OPT, Llama-3.1, and Qwen2.5) and public benchmark data sets. The work involves no human subjects, no newly collected data, and no private or personally identifiable information. Lowering the memory required for fine-tuning broadens access to model adaptation; this carries the dual-use considerations common to all fine-tuning methods, since adapted models can serve beneficial or harmful ends, but our method introduces no risk beyond that of existing fine-tuning approaches.

The proposed methods are fully specified: ZO-RGD in Algorithm 1 (Section 4.3 ) and ZO-RGD-S in Algorithm 2 (Appendix A.3 ), with the stored representation, initialization, retraction, and per-step cost detailed in Appendix A . All assumptions underlying the theoretical results are stated in Section 5 and Appendix C.2 ; complete proofs of the propositions and of the convergence theorem are given in Appendices B and C , respectively. The evaluation protocol is described in Section 6.1 and Appendix D.1 , compute resources in Appendix D.2 , and per-seed values in Appendix D.7 . All experiments use publicly available pretrained models and public data sets. The source code will be released upon acceptance, together with a manifest that maps every reported cell to its job configuration, selection rule, seeds, hardware, and completion status, including failed runs.

chunks.section: Appendix A Algorithmic and Implementation Details
chunks.text: This appendix follows the order of Section 4 : the thin-SVD representation (Appendix A.1 ), the near-zero initialization of the fixed-rank state (Appendix A.2 ), the full pseudocode of ZO-RGD-S (Appendix A.3 ), and the complexity of the implementation (Appendix A.4 ).

The optimization variable is the matrix Δ ​ 𝑾 ℓ \Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{\ell} itself, and the stored thin-SVD triple ( 𝑼 ℓ , 𝚺 ℓ , 𝑽 ℓ ) (\boldsymbol{U}_{\ell},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell},\boldsymbol{V}_{\ell}) is a numerical representation of that point. The representation is unique only up to simultaneous sign changes of paired singular vectors, and, when singular values coincide, up to joint rotations of the corresponding subspaces. None of this affects the algorithm or the analysis, because projection, normalization, and retraction depend on the represented point only: they are invariant to the choice of representative. This is the precise sense in which the method has no factor-gauge degrees of freedom, in contrast to optimizing LoRA factor coordinates ( 𝑩 , 𝑨 ) (\boldsymbol{B},\boldsymbol{A}) .

The fixed-rank constraint excludes the zero update when r ℓ > 0 r_{\ell}>0 . To preserve the pretrained initialization while remaining feasible for ZO-RGD and ZO-RGD-S, we initialize each trainable update block at a near-zero fixed-rank point: Δ ​ 𝑾 init , ℓ = 𝑼 init , ℓ ​ ( σ init , ℓ ​ 𝑰 r ℓ ) ​ 𝑽 init , ℓ ⊤ , ℓ ∈ 𝒮 , \displaystyle\Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{init},\ell}=\boldsymbol{U}_{\mathrm{init},\ell}(\sigma_{\mathrm{init},\ell}\boldsymbol{I}_{r_{\ell}})\boldsymbol{V}_{\mathrm{init},\ell}^{\top},\qquad\ell\in\mathcal{S}, (19) where 0 < σ init , ℓ ≪ 1 0<\sigma_{\mathrm{init},\ell}\ll 1 , and 𝑼 init , ℓ \boldsymbol{U}_{\mathrm{init},\ell} and 𝑽 init , ℓ \boldsymbol{V}_{\mathrm{init},\ell} have orthonormal columns. The factors are obtained by QR orthonormalization of Gaussian matrices (computed in single precision and cast to the model precision), and σ init , ℓ = 10 − 6 \sigma_{\mathrm{init},\ell}=10^{-6} by default. This keeps each update block on its prescribed fixed-rank manifold while making 𝑾 0 + Δ ​ 𝑾 init \boldsymbol{W}_{0}+\Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{\mathrm{init}} numerically close to the pretrained model.

Algorithm 2 expands the scalar recursion in ( 14 ). As in Algorithm 1 , the pseudocode shows the matrix-block updates. Algorithm 2 ZO-RGD-S 1: Frozen weights 𝑾 0 \boldsymbol{W}_{0} ; initial update Δ ​ 𝑾 0 ∈ ℳ \Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{0}\in\mathcal{M} ; learning rate η \eta ; perturbation radius ϵ \epsilon ; smoothing parameter β ∈ [ 0 , 1 ) \beta\in[0,1) . 2: Fix an order ℓ 1 , … , ℓ K \ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{K} of the trainable matrix blocks. 3: for t = 0 , 1 , 2 , … t=0,1,2,\ldots do 4: Sample a realization ξ t \xi_{t} , construct normalized tangent random matrices, and compute s ^ t \hat{s}_{t} with the same two forward passes as ZO-RGD. 5: if t = 0 t=0 then 6: m 0 , 0 = s ^ 0 m_{0,0}=\hat{s}_{0} . 7: else 8: m t , 0 = m t − 1 , K m_{t,0}=m_{t-1,K} . 9: end if 10: for k = 1 , … , K k=1,\ldots,K do 11: m t , k = β ​ m t , k − 1 + ( 1 − β ) ​ s ^ t m_{t,k}=\beta m_{t,k-1}+(1-\beta)\hat{s}_{t} . 12: 𝑮 ^ t , ℓ k S = m t , k ​ 𝒁 ~ t , ℓ k \widehat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{t,\ell_{k}}=m_{t,k}\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}_{t,\ell_{k}} . 13: Δ ​ 𝑾 t + 1 , ℓ k = ℛ Δ ​ 𝑾 t , ℓ k ​ ( − η ​ 𝑮 ^ t , ℓ k S ) \Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{t+1,\ell_{k}}=\mathcal{R}_{\Delta\boldsymbol{W}_{t,\ell_{k}}}(-\eta\widehat{\boldsymbol{G}}^{\mathrm{S}}_{t,\ell_{k}}) . 14: end for 15: end for
Two costs are distinguished: the persistent trainable state and the per-step work.

At each selected two-dimensional block, the trainable update is stored as the thin-SVD triple ( 𝑼 ℓ , 𝚺 ℓ , 𝑽 ℓ ) (\boldsymbol{U}_{\ell},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell},\boldsymbol{V}_{\ell}) , with 𝑼 ℓ ∈ ℝ m ℓ × r ℓ \boldsymbol{U}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}} , diagonal 𝚺 ℓ ∈ ℝ r ℓ × r ℓ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{r_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}} , and 𝑽 ℓ ∈ ℝ n ℓ × r ℓ \boldsymbol{V}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times r_{\ell}} . The per-block state therefore has r ℓ ​ ( m ℓ + n ℓ + 1 ) r_{\ell}(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell}+1) parameters, i.e. O ⁡ ( ( m ℓ + n ℓ ) ​ r ℓ ) O((m_{\ell}+n_{\ell})r_{\ell}) , much smaller than a dense m ℓ ​ n ℓ m_{\ell}n_{\ell} trainable update when r ℓ ≪ min ⁡ ( m ℓ , n ℓ ) r_{\ell}\ll\min(m_{\ell},n_{\ell}) . The training loop stores no first-order optimizer state and no backpropagation graph; random matrices are regenerated from seeds, and the thin-SVD triple is the only trainable representation. ZO-RGD-S adds only a scalar smoothing variable and does not maintain a matrix-valued momentum buffer. Thus the forward-only memory profile remains in the MeZO/LOZO regime, with an additional fixed-rank update state that scales linearly in rank; Appendix D.17 quantifies this state for OPT-1.3B.

The per-step work, however, is not low-rank: the current implementation materializes dense m ℓ × n ℓ m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell} intermediates, the Gaussian random matrix, its tangent projection, and the update direction, so each block incurs O ⁡ ( m ℓ ​ n ℓ ​ r ℓ ) O(m_{\ell}n_{\ell}r_{\ell}) work in the projection and retraction products plus O ⁡ ( m ℓ ​ n ℓ ) O(m_{\ell}n_{\ell}) transient memory, in addition to the two forward passes; only the core SVD of the retraction is small ( 2 ​ r ℓ × 2 ​ r ℓ 2r_{\ell}\times 2r_{\ell} ). In two allocations on different A100-80G chips, profiling all methods back to back gives roughly 1.8 × 1.8\times the per-step time of LOZO at the identical forward-pass count (Table 6 ). Projection and retraction add computation while retaining comparable peak memory. A fused factored application that samples random matrices directly in factor coordinates could avoid the dense intermediates in principle, but it is an engineering change we have not implemented or measured, and a “lazy” retraction applied every few steps would change the algorithm itself (intermediate iterates would leave the manifold and random matrices would use a stale tangent space), requiring its own bias and convergence analysis.

chunks.section: Appendix C Convergence Analysis of ZO-RGD
chunks.text: This appendix proves the results of Section 5 for ZO-RGD exactly as implemented: the mixed product of fixed-rank blocks and a Euclidean factor of one-dimensional parameters, blockwise normalized tangent random matrices, one shared finite-difference scalar per step, ambient tangent-line evaluation points, and update-only truncated-SVD retraction. Proposition 2 is the single-block specialization of Lemmas 1 – 3 . Throughout, “ZO-RGD” means the base method of Algorithm 1 with one joint random direction per step, zero weight decay, no singular-value clamping, no gradient accumulation, and a differentiable training loss.

The trainable two-dimensional blocks are indexed by ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , N } \ell\in\{1,\ldots,N\} ; block ℓ \ell has ambient shape m ℓ × n ℓ m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell} and fixed rank 1 ≤ r ℓ ≤ min ⁡ ( m ℓ , n ℓ ) 1\leq r_{\ell}\leq\min(m_{\ell},n_{\ell}) . (Throughout, N N is the block count; the symbol L L is reserved for the gradient-Lipschitz constant of Assumption 2 , and ρ 3 \rho_{3} for its third-derivative constant, distinct from the normalization radii ρ ℓ \rho_{\ell} .) Write ℳ ℓ := ℳ r ℓ m ℓ × n ℓ \mathcal{M}_{\ell}:=\mathcal{M}_{r_{\ell}}^{m_{\ell}\times n_{\ell}} for the fixed-rank manifold of block ℓ \ell , d ℓ := dim ℳ ℓ = r ℓ ​ ( m ℓ + n ℓ − r ℓ ) , ρ ℓ 2 := m ℓ ​ n ℓ , c ℓ := ρ ℓ 2 d ℓ . \displaystyle d_{\ell}:=\dim\mathcal{M}_{\ell}=r_{\ell}(m_{\ell}+n_{\ell}-r_{\ell}),\qquad\rho_{\ell}^{2}:=m_{\ell}n_{\ell},\qquad c_{\ell}:=\frac{\rho_{\ell}^{2}}{d_{\ell}}. The trainable one-dimensional parameters (biases and LayerNorm parameters) form one Euclidean factor ℝ d 0 \mathbb{R}^{d_{0}} ; set c 0 := 1 c_{0}:=1 . c ℓ ≥ 1 c_{\ell}\geq 1 , because m ℓ ​ n ℓ − d ℓ = ( m ℓ − r ℓ ) ​ ( n ℓ − r ℓ ) ≥ 0 m_{\ell}n_{\ell}-d_{\ell}=(m_{\ell}-r_{\ell})(n_{\ell}-r_{\ell})\geq 0 , with equality if and only if r ℓ = min ⁡ ( m ℓ , n ℓ ) r_{\ell}=\min(m_{\ell},n_{\ell}) .

chunks.text: (a) Regular region. Each ℳ ℓ \mathcal{M}_{\ell} is non-compact: its closure adds the rank-deficient boundary, on which the tangent spaces and the retraction degenerate. Assumption 1 confines the analysis to a region away from that boundary; it does not prove that the iterates stay there. This is the standard form of assumption in fixed-rank optimization ( Vandereycken, 2013 ; Schneider and Uschmajew, 2015 ) . This appendix follows the order of Section 6 . Appendices D.1 and D.2 give the training protocol and compute resources. Appendices D.3 – D.6 supplement the broad-suite comparison with the complete OPT-1.3B table, its unified-protocol rerun, the trainability floor, and the OPT-30B spot-check. Appendices D.7 – D.9 supplement the controlled comparison with per-seed values, the matched-rank comparison, and a shared-learning-rate regime with convergence against forward passes. Appendix D.10 gives the learning-rate diagnostic for the modern-model panel. Appendices D.11 – D.15 collect the geometry controls, negative results, ablations, and stability diagnostics; Appendices D.16 and D.17 give runtime and memory; and Appendix D.18 is the failure register.

For ZO-RGD and ZO-RGD-S, each ZO update uses one normalized tangent random matrix, so the two-point finite-difference scalar is obtained with two forward passes. Unless otherwise noted, runs use FP16 checkpoints, 20,000 20{,}000 training steps, constant learning rate, ϵ = 10 − 3 \epsilon=10^{-3} , and weight decay 0 0 . Seeds are paired: the training-subset seed and the trainer seed move together. Hyperparameter selection uses a dedicated grid seed ( 0 0 ) on OPT and a disjoint pilot seed ( 7 7 ) on the modern-model panel; report seeds are { 1 , 2 , 3 } \{1,2,3\} on the OPT panels and { 0 , 1 , 2 } \{0,1,2\} on the modern-model panel (the two panels were executed independently; neither report set overlaps its selection seed, and the per-panel seed sets are disclosed here because they differ). Each run samples three disjoint subsets with the paired seeds: up to 1000 1000 training examples, up to 500 500 development examples held out from the training data ( 100 100 for CB and COPA), and up to 1000 1000 evaluation examples from the task’s validation split; smaller datasets are capped by the available split sizes, and reported n n is the actual subset size of the run. Training operates only on the training subset. Within each run, the kept checkpoint is the one with the lowest development loss ( eval_loss ), under the same cadence for every method; development loss is the selection quantity because it is the only development-set signal produced by every trainer in the comparison, so a single selection rule can be applied symmetrically. The evaluation subset is read exactly once per run, after all selection. Table 7 summarizes the per-method configurations, and Table 8 audits the baseline implementations and their deviations.

chunks.text: LOZO accumulated-update rank. The fixed-rank constraint is a real restriction on the update only because the closest baseline’s persistent update is not rank-limited in practice. The baseline’s learned update is effectively half full-rank; ours is exactly rank r r . HiZOO released-implementation diagnostic. We include HiZOO ( Zhao et al., 2024b ) in the OPT-13B RTE comparison and convergence plot using the released implementation at the shared learning rate 10 − 7 10^{-7} . At its published OPT learning rate, however, the same implementation scores at chance on our RTE setup at both 1.3B and 13B ( 52.1 ± 3.8 52.1\pm 3.8 / 52.5 ± 1.1 52.5\pm 1.1 ). Instrumentation shows that its Hessian-information coefficient is inactive ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ) in the released setting, at which point the update rule reduces to MeZO’s; matched-learning-rate comparisons overlap with MeZO within seed noise at both scales. A modified activated configuration ( α > 0 \alpha>0 , FP32 Hessian state) trains in smoke tests, but it is not the published configuration and is therefore not substituted for the released method in the main comparison.

chunks.section: D.11 Additional geometry controls and negative results
chunks.text: Negative results on our own variants. Two internal variants underperform and are reported as such. A tangent-space (matrix) momentum variant loses to the scalar recursion of ZO-RGD-S on four of six tasks at three paired seeds (pilot: one of six, mean − 2.0 -2.0 points), and a per-step EMA variant wins on one of three tasks; the scalar recursion along the fixed traversal order remains the recommended smoothing. A lazy-retraction variant (retract every F F steps, F ∈ { 10 , 50 , 200 } F\in\{10,50,200\} ) is slower than retracting every step by 17 17 – 19 % 19\% : phase profiling shows retraction is only 18.4 % 18.4\% of a step while random-matrix generation and projection account for ≈ 60 % \approx 60\% , and deferring retraction forces materialization of the accumulated update. Lazy retraction is a separate algorithm outside the scope of the base theorem, and its measured effect is negative on both axes; runtime engineering should target the random-matrix generation and projection phases instead.

chunks.section: D.12 Effect of normalizing the tangent random matrix
chunks.text: We test the central design choice of the estimator: post-projection normalization that restores the ambient finite-difference radius after tangent projection. Without normalization, the raw projected random matrix has Frobenius norm concentrated at d r \sqrt{d_{r}} rather than m ​ n \sqrt{mn} . For OPT-1.3B square blocks with m = n = 2048 m=n=2048 and r = 4 r=4 , the ratio is d r / ( m ​ n ) ≈ 0.063 \sqrt{d_{r}/(mn)}\approx 0.063 , so the unnormalized two-point finite difference evaluates the loss within an effective radius of about 6 % 6\% of the standard MeZO/LOZO scale at the same ϵ \epsilon . Table 19 reports controlled OPT-1.3B ablations with ZO-RGD ( r = 4 r=4 , η = 10 − 7 \eta=10^{-7} , batch size 16 16 , 20 20 K steps). The first comparison uses the raw projected random matrix at ϵ = 10 − 3 \epsilon=10^{-3} on SST-2, RTE, and SQuAD; the rescaled-radius comparison uses ϵ = 1.6 × 10 − 2 \epsilon=1.6\times 10^{-2} , the square-block compensation value, to test whether one global radius can replace per-block normalization. A rerun cannot repair it: with normalization off, the SQuAD ablation diverges deterministically (first evaluation NaN on all seeds; Appendix D.18 ), and the divergence itself is the ablation conclusion.

Building on this fixed-rank update trajectory, we propose a forward-only Riemannian ZO fine-tuning framework.
